nameStory: This plant gets its common name from its most striking feature - bright blue berries that look like perfect little beads adorning the forest floor. The scientific name honors DeWitt Clinton, a naturalist and former governor of New York who championed nature exploration in the early 1800s.
description: Bluebead lily is a charming woodland wildflower that creates distinctive clusters of broad, glossy leaves rising directly from the forest floor. Each plant typically grows 6-15 inches tall with 2-4 oval leaves that look almost tropical in their lushness. In late spring, it produces small yellow flowers on a central stalk, followed by its signature bright blue berries that persist into fall.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Brilliant blue berries, about the size of large peas, cluster at the top of the stem - they're so bright they almost seem to glow against the dark forest floor

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: 2-4 broad, oval leaves with smooth edges and parallel veins, feeling thick and almost rubbery to the touch, arranged in a basal rosette

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small, nodding yellow flowers with 6 petals, appearing in clusters of 3-8 on a single stem rising above the leaves in May-June

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms colonies of individual plants emerging from underground rhizomes, creating patches of identical-looking rosettes across the forest floor

habitat: Thrives in cool, moist, acidic soils of northern hardwood and coniferous forests throughout New England's mountains and cooler regions. Look for it in the understory of maple-birch-beech forests or mixed woods with hemlock and spruce, often on slopes or near streams where the soil stays consistently moist.

seasonality.spring: Bright yellow flowers appear in May-June, nodding gracefully above the emerging glossy leaves. This is when the plant is most noticeable before the berries develop.
seasonality.summer: Flowers fade and the distinctive bright blue berries begin forming in July-August, gradually reaching their full brilliant color.
seasonality.fall: Blue berries are at their most vibrant and persist well into autumn, making this the easiest season for identification even as leaves begin to yellow.
seasonality.winter: Plants die back completely, leaving no above-ground trace until the following spring's emergence from underground rhizomes.

funFact: Despite being called 'bluebead lily,' some botanists argue it should really be called 'yellow clintonia' because it's actually the only species in its genus with yellow flowers - all its relatives have white or greenish blooms, making the flower color more unique than the blue berries!
confusionNotes: The broad, parallel-veined leaves might remind you of wild leeks (ramps), but bluebead lily leaves are much thicker and more oval-shaped, plus they lack that distinctive oniony smell when crushed. The blue berries are absolutely distinctive - no other New England wildflower produces anything quite like them.
contextualKnowledge: This plant has several confusing common names that can trip up beginners. 'Poisonberry' and 'snakeberry' refer to the berries being inedible (though not seriously toxic), while 'corn lily' comes from the leaf shape. Some sources call it 'Clinton's lily' after DeWitt Clinton, but 'bluebead lily' remains the most widely recognized name.
compareHints: Bluebead lily is the only member of the Clintonia genus in New England, making it unique in our region. Within the lily family, it's most similar to trout lilies, but those have mottled leaves and completely different yellow flowers that face upward rather than nodding downward. The combination of broad basal leaves and bright blue berries makes bluebead lily unmistakable among New England wildflowers.
